What helps children learn in Pialand’s primary schools?

Findings from the national census of all 500 public primary schools — what they mean for the Ministry of Education, and where UNICEF comes in.

Karen Avanesian

a census of all 500 public primary schools learning score, 0–100 8 school characteristics

⏱ SLIDE 1 — 0:45 · move on at 0:45

Good morning. The Ministry gave us something rare: data on every public primary school in the country. All 500 of them. Each school has a learning score from 0 to 100, and eight facts about the school.

Ten minutes, three questions. What did we find. What should the Ministry do. And how can UNICEF help.

One thing before we start: this is one year of data. So everything I show is a pattern, not proof of cause.

Say: “Here is the whole school system in one picture” — and move.

If you run behind later, win time back on slides 5 and 7. Never cut slides 2 or 6.

Pialand does not have one school system — it has several

The chart starts empty — on purpose. Every square will be one school. Best schools at the top, weakest at the bottom.

[CLICK 1] These are the weakest 100 schools in the country — the bottom fifth. Almost all of them rural.

[CLICK 2] Only a few are urban — the outlined ones. So: 100 schools, average score 37 — half the national level. And 58 of these 100 sit in just two regions: 14 and 16. Remember those two.

[CLICK 5] Now the best part. The glowing blue squares: 42 rural schools scoring 90 or more. Same conditions, ordinary resources — top of the country. Rural does not mean doomed. Keep these 42 in mind.

[CLICK 6] The scores side by side: the country averages 70. The bottom hundred: 37.

[CLICK 7] And those 42 schools are the proof this can be fixed.

⏱ SLIDE 3 — 0:55 · move on at 3:15 · 2 clicks

Rural schools average 68, compared with 79 in urban schools. A gap of about six points remains after accounting for the school characteristics recorded in the census.

[CLICK 1] The regional picture helps us decide where to focus. In several regions, rural schools score substantially below urban schools.

[CLICK 2] In Regions 14 and 16, both groups average around 63. Support there needs to include struggling urban schools as well.

So geography helps us identify priorities, but the final selection should use each school’s needs. A rural label alone is too broad: almost four in five schools are rural.

Schools led by women have higher learning scores

FINDING 03 COMPARING OTHERWISE SIMILAR SCHOOLS — AND STRESS-TESTING THE HEADLINE

No clear link to learning in this data:  internet connectivity · pupil–teacher ratio · maths textbooks · committee training

Good news: female-led schools show the strongest advantage. To act on it we first need to understand it — the census says nothing about qualifications or experience.

22%
vs 4%
Women lead 22% of urban schools and 4% of rural schools.
+9.5
Yet within rural schools alone the advantage persists (+9.5 points, 15 schools) — and it is the same size in both settings. “They are simply urban” does not explain it.
38
Only 38 female-led schools in the country — and heads are not appointed at random. Selective appointment cannot be ruled out. A lead to investigate, not a staffing instruction.

CAUTION — associations, not causes; qualifications and experience unobserved. Consistent with UNICEF Innocenti & IIEP’s Women in Learning Leadership (WiLL) research: women hold ~1 in 10 school leaderships in parts of Africa, and female leaders appear to adopt different practices.

9%
The eight recorded characteristics explain 9% of score differences. Most variation remains unexplained.

differences shown after holding the other measured characteristics constant full model results in the written briefing annex

⏱ SLIDE 4 — 1:20 · move on at 4:35

There is also an encouraging finding. Schools led by women score about nine points higher after accounting for the other recorded characteristics. The difference also appears within rural schools. Schools with more female teachers tend to score higher too; the reading-book result is less certain.

Women’s leadership is a potential strength to build on. We need to understand what these schools do differently. There are only 38 women headteachers in the data, and we have no information on their qualifications or experience. Comparing their practices will help us identify what to test elsewhere.

For internet, pupil–teacher ratios, maths textbooks and committee training, the analysis finds no clear relationship with scores. That does not establish that these resources are ineffective.

Together, the eight characteristics explain less than a tenth of score differences. We need to investigate teaching and school management directly.

Before the recommendations — one honest question.

Support all 500 schools — or the most vulnerable first?

THE STRATEGIC CHOICE EVERY PROGRAMME MUST ANSWER THIS BEFORE MONEY MOVES

OPTION A — SUPPORT EVERYONE

One national programme, all 500 schools

An equal allocation spreads additional funding across all 500 schools. Schools with greater needs may require more intensive support.

The same additional allocation for every school.
OPTION B — MOST VULNERABLE FIRST

Start with the 100 lowest-scoring schools

Prioritise the 100 lowest-scoring schools, subject to checking enrolment and other indicators of need.

Average score 37/100; 88 are rural and 58 are in Regions 14 and 16.

Our read: start with the most vulnerable — and cost it honestly. Remote schools cost more to reach — logistics, supervision, teacher incentives — so this choice needs real numbers, not slogans. That costing is exactly where UNICEF comes in.

schools weighted equally — enrolment per school is not in the census either path needs a costing before money moves

⏱ SLIDE 5 — 1:05 · move on at 5:40

Does the Ministry support all 500 schools equally — or start with the most vulnerable?

I recommend using the next round of additional funding to prioritise the lowest-scoring schools.

The bottom hundred are a starting point. Before finalising the list, the Ministry should check enrolment and other indicators of need. Schools just above the cutoff may also require support.

The 42 outliers prove rural schools can reach the top. This is the idea behind positive deviance: identifying schools that do better than others in similar circumstances, then studying what they do differently.

A targeted programme can provide more intensive support, but we need to budget for reaching remote schools. Basic provision across the system should continue.

What we recommend to the Ministry

RECOMMENDATIONS THREE MOVES, SEQUENCED — AND ONE THING TO HOLD OFF ON

R1 · TARGET

Support schools by need, not uniformly

Prioritise additional support using low scores and verified school needs, with particular attention to rural schools and Regions 14 and 16.

Why: two divides in the data — rural schools trail urban ones, and two regions trail the whole country.
R2 · LEARN

Study the outliers — and what drives the gaps

Compare selected high-scoring rural schools with schools in similar circumstances; identify practices to test.

Why: 42 rural schools score 90+, but the census does not explain how they achieve those results.
R3 · STAFF

Study leadership practices and barriers to rural headship

Study leadership practices and address barriers to women becoming rural headteachers.

Why: higher scores in female-led schools warrant investigation; women lead only 4% of rural schools.

Before investing: assess school needs before committing to a national investment programme. This census does not establish which inputs improve learning.

recommendations follow the three findings one-to-one gender patterns treated as associations, not causes

⏱ SLIDE 6 — 1:20 · move on at 7:00 · 4 clicks

[CLICK 1] Target. Put the next round of support where the gaps are: rural schools everywhere, particularly those with high enrolment, and Regions 14 and 16 as whole regions.

[CLICK 2] Learn. Select a sample of the 42 high-scoring rural schools and compare them with schools in similar circumstances. Identify differences in teaching, attendance and school management that we can test elsewhere.

[CLICK 3] Women leaders. Treat this as an asset. Study what female-led schools do differently, spread what works, and open the way for women to lead rural schools — today it is four percent. What we do NOT recommend: moving heads around by gender.

[CLICK 4] For new spending, require a clear explanation of the problem each investment will address. This census alone cannot justify a national purchasing programme or cuts to essential resources.

From findings to a financed programme — the Ministry owns it

UNICEF’S ROLE MINISTRY-LED AT EVERY STEP — UNICEF BRINGS METHOD, EVIDENCE AND COSTING

1
DIAGNOSE
A national team appointed by the Ministry leads; UNICEF brings the method. The outlier-schools study (Data Must Speak) and the paired study of female- and male-led schools, building on Innocenti & IIEP’s WiLL research — on data the Ministry already owns.
→
2
DESIGN & COST
Co-design with the Ministry, then run the cost–benefit analysis: cost per learning point, targeted vs universal, remoteness premium included — the number a Ministry of Finance acts on.
→
3
PILOT & EVALUATE
The Ministry runs the pilot in Regions 14 and 16; UNICEF builds in rigorous evaluation from day one — so scale-up is evidence, not hope.
→
4
MAINSTREAM
What works becomes the norm. We support the Ministry in scaling where needed — we build capacity, help plan the roll-out, and stay alongside during implementation.

assumptions — one-year snapshot: associations, not causes · learning score taken as reliable & SDG 4.1.1-consistent · schools weighted equally · regions from School ID · head appointments not random

⏱ SLIDE 7 — 2:10 · move on at 9:10 · 3 clicks

Here is how I would organise the work.

The Ministry appoints a team to lead the diagnosis. It verifies the school list and region codes, then visits selected schools to observe lessons and interview teachers and headteachers. UNICEF supports the study design, drawing on Data Must Speak and the Women in Learning Leadership research. The output is a short list of practices and constraints to address.

[CLICK 1] The team then selects a small number of measures to test. These might include classroom coaching or support for headteachers, depending on the findings. For each measure, specify who delivers it, how often and at what cost. Include travel to remote schools. UNICEF supports the costing and comparison of options. This produces a costed pilot proposal for the Ministry to approve.

[CLICK 2] The Ministry runs the pilot in selected schools in Regions 14 and 16 (once the geographic coding is confirmed). UNICEF helps set up the evaluation before delivery starts. Measure learning at the start and end, use suitable comparison schools, and track costs and whether the support actually reaches schools.

[CLICK 3] The Ministry then decides what to expand, revise or stop. Expansion should depend on improved learning and affordable delivery. Put the measures that work into the Ministry’s budget and routine support to schools, extending them where needed. UNICEF helps prepare training and supervision guidance for district teams.

The census tells us where to look. The 42 outliers tell us what to look for.

Every number here can be traced back to the data — one script, fully reproducible.

Thank you. Questions.

If asked — why do women-led schools do better? We do not know yet: nothing in the data on qualifications or experience. That is why the study comes first. What will it cost? The studies are nearly free — the data exists; pricing the support package is step two. Can we trust the score? We take it as given — we cannot check it from one file; that is why better measurement is part of the offer. Is the unexplained 90% just other school factors? Yes — unexplained means unexplained: teaching, children’s backgrounds, community, noise. These data cannot split it; the studies are how we find out.
